title: Choking Incident Involving Plush Educational Toy Battery Cover
premise: A toddler in suburban Chicago choked on a small battery compartment cover that popped off a plush educational toy during bedtime reading.

side_A.role: an advocate at a consumer-safety group
side_A.goal: pushing for a recall of the product

side_B.goal: showing the product is safe when used as directed

documents:
=== DOCUMENT 1: Incident Log and Paramedic Field Report ===

**INCIDENT REPORT: CHOKING EVENT**
**Date:** October 14, 2023
**Time:** 20:15
**Location:** 4242 Ridge Ave, Evanston, Illinois
**Responding Unit:** Evanston Fire Department, Squad 4

**I. INITIAL RESPONSE AND PATIENT STATUS**
Upon arrival at the residence, paramedic J. Miller observed a toddler, identified as the child of the household, seated on the living room carpet. The child was exhibiting signs of acute airway obstruction, including high-pitched stridor and inability to cry. The child’s age was verified by the parent as 2 years and 4 months. The object causing the obstruction was identified as a hard plastic component from an educational plush toy.

**II. RESCUE PROCEDURES**
Paramedic J. Miller administered back blows to clear the airway. A total of 15 back blows were delivered over a duration of approximately 45 seconds until the airway was fully cleared and the child began to cough. The child’s respiratory function returned to baseline immediately following the final blow. No CPR was required. The child was monitored for 20 minutes on-scene and showed no signs of distress or secondary injury.

**III. SCENE OBSERVATIONS**
The object in question was a small, circular plastic cover. It was located on the living room carpet, approximately 3 feet from the child’s seated position. The component appears to be a battery compartment cover.

**IV. PRODUCT IDENTIFICATION**
The associated toy is a plush educational device. The model number "EduPlush-300" is visible on the base panel. The manufacturer is BrightMind Toys Inc. The toy consists of soft polyester fabric and hard plastic components. The battery compartment is secured by two screws.

**V. WITNESS STATEMENTS (PRELIMINARY)**
**Parent (Marcus Thorne):** Stated that the child was reading the toy’s accompanying storybook when the cover detached. The parent reported that the toy was functioning normally without any prior signs of damage. The parent noted that the toy was purchased from a local retail store on September 2, 2023.

**Babysitter (Elena Ross):** Stated that the child was handling the toy with both hands when the cover popped off.

**VI. PRODUCT DOCUMENTATION REVIEW**
**Packaging Label:** The toy’s original packaging displays a warning label stating "Not for children under 3 years old."
**User Manual:** The manual states that the battery compartment should be checked weekly for tightness.
**Manufacturer Claim:** BrightMind Toys Inc. states that the toy passed all federal small parts testing in Q2 2023.
**Screw Specifications:** The battery compartment screws are rated for a minimum torque of 0.5 Nm.

**VII. MEASUREMENTS**
The detached battery cover was measured at the scene.
*   Diameter: 1.2 inches
*   Thickness: 0.1 inches

**VIII. CONCLUSION**
The incident resulted in a temporary airway obstruction. The cause of the detachment is under investigation. The child was transported to Evanston Hospital for observation but was released the following morning.

=== DOCUMENT 2: Witness Statement of Marcus Thorne ===

**STATEMENT OF WITNESS: MARCUS THORNE**
**Role:** Consumer Safety Analyst / Parent of Child
**Date of Statement:** October 15, 2023

I am writing to provide my account of the choking incident that occurred in my home on October 14, 2023, at 8:15 PM. My child, who is 2 years and 4 months old, was in the living room with his babysitter, Elena Ross.

I want to be clear that this was not a case of negligence on the part of the child, but a failure of the product design. The toy in question is the EduPlush-300, manufactured by BrightMind Toys Inc. We purchased this toy from a local retail store on September 2, 2023. The receipt confirms that the toy was purchased with the full battery compartment cover attached. The toy has been in continuous use by the family for 42 days prior to the incident.

At the time of the incident, my child was reading the toy's accompanying storybook. The battery compartment cover was removed from the toy's base panel during the incident. I was in the next room when I heard the commotion. When I rushed into the living room, I saw Elena Ross frantically trying to help my child. The cover was lying on the carpet, 3 feet from where my child had been sitting.

I have reviewed the technical specifications and I am certain that the battery cover detached due to a manufacturing defect in the screw threads, which were stripped upon removal. The screws are rated for a minimum torque of 0.5 Nm, yet they failed completely. It is my professional assessment that the threads were compromised from the start.

Furthermore, I must address the supervision. The babysitter was not actively supervising the child at the moment of detachment, as she was adjusting the lighting in the room. This lack of attention allowed the incident to escalate. If she had been paying attention, she might have prevented the child from putting the object in his mouth.

I also take issue with the age appropriateness of this product. The toy's marketing materials explicitly targeted children aged 2-5, making the 'under 3' warning contradictory and misleading. The packaging says "Not for children under 3 years old," yet the marketing suggests it is suitable for my 2-year-old. This is a dangerous contradiction that misled us into believing the toy was safe for our child.

I believe the battery compartment screws were already loose before the incident, as evidenced by the cover popping off without significant external force. The toy's user manual states that the battery compartment should be checked weekly for tightness, but this is an unreasonable burden on a parent to monitor such a small component in a soft plush toy.

I am requesting a full investigation into the manufacturing defects of the EduPlush-300 and the misleading marketing practices of BrightMind Toys Inc.

=== DOCUMENT 3: Witness Statement of Sarah Jenkins ===

**STATEMENT OF WITNESS: SARAH JENKINS**
**Role:** Head of Communications, BrightMind Toys Inc.
**Date of Statement:** October 15, 2023

I am submitting this statement on behalf of BrightMind Toys Inc. regarding the incident involving the EduPlush-300 educational plush toy on October 14, 2023. We are committed to the safety of children and have reviewed all available data.

First, regarding the cause of the detachment: The battery cover detached because the babysitter applied excessive force while attempting to open the compartment, causing the screws to back out. It is important to note that the battery compartment is secured by two screws rated for a minimum torque of 0.5 Nm. These screws are designed to be secure and require specific tools to remove. The fact that the cover popped off suggests that external force was applied, likely by the babysitter, rather than a manufacturing defect.

We also want to address the adequacy of supervision. The babysitter, Elena Ross, was seated directly next to the child and had clear visual and physical access to intervene immediately. It is not true that she was adjusting the lighting. She was present and attentive. The incident occurred because the child handled the toy in a manner not intended for the product.

Regarding the age appropriateness of the product: The toy's marketing materials consistently displayed the 'under 3' warning on all primary packaging and online listings. The warning label stating "Not for children under 3 years old" is prominently displayed on the packaging. We have not targeted children aged 2-5 in our primary marketing channels for this specific model. Any confusion regarding the age range is due to misinterpretation of the general educational category, not specific marketing for toddlers under 3.

We also confirm that the battery compartment screws were tight and secure before the incident, as confirmed by the parent's prior inspection logs. The parent is aware of the user manual, which states that the battery compartment should be checked weekly for tightness. We stand by the integrity of our product.

BrightMind Toys Inc. states that the toy passed all federal small parts testing in Q2 2023. The material composition includes soft polyester fabric and hard plastic components, which are standard for educational toys. The toy was purchased from a local retail store on September 2, 2023, and the retail store receipt shows the toy was purchased with the full battery compartment cover attached.

We believe this incident is the result of improper use and external force, not a product defect. We are reviewing the incident to ensure our safety protocols are being communicated effectively to parents.

=== DOCUMENT 5: Email Correspondence Between Thorne and BrightMind Toys ===

**Email 1**
**From:** Marcus Thorne <m.thorne@example.com>
**To:** support@brightmindtoys.com
**Subject:** Incident with EduPlush-300 - Request for Investigation
**Date:** October 15, 2023

To BrightMind Toys Support,

I am writing regarding a serious incident that occurred on October 14, 2023, involving your EduPlush-300 toy. My 2-year-old child choked on the battery compartment cover, which detached from the toy. The cover measured 1.2 inches in diameter and was found on the carpet.

I believe this is a manufacturing defect. The screws were stripped, and the cover popped off without significant force. The toy was purchased on September 2, 2023, and has been in use for 42 days. The babysitter, Elena Ross, was adjusting the lighting and was not actively supervising the child at the moment of detachment.

The marketing materials targeted children aged 2-5, which contradicts the "under 3" warning. This is misleading. I request a full investigation and a recall if necessary.

Regards,
Marcus Thorne

**Email 2**
**From:** Sarah Jenkins <s.jenkins@brightmindtoys.com>
**To:** Marcus Thorne <m.thorne@example.com>
**Subject:** RE: Incident with EduPlush-300 - Request for Investigation
**Date:** October 16, 2023

Dear Mr. Thorne,

Thank you for contacting us. We are deeply concerned about the incident involving your child. We have reviewed your report and the incident log.

We would like to clarify that the battery cover detached because the babysitter applied excessive force while attempting to open the compartment, causing the screws to back out. The screws are rated for a minimum torque of 0.5 Nm and are designed to be secure. We do not believe there is a manufacturing defect.

Regarding supervision, our records indicate that the babysitter was seated directly next to the child and had clear visual and physical access. We do not have evidence that she was adjusting the lighting.

We also want to clarify that our marketing materials consistently displayed the 'under 3' warning on all primary packaging and online listings. We have not targeted children aged 2-5. The toy passed all federal small parts testing in Q2 2023.

We stand by the safety of our product. We recommend following the user manual, which states that the battery compartment should be checked weekly for tightness. Your inspection logs show that the screws were tight and secure prior to the incident.

Sincerely,
Sarah Jenkins
Head of Communications, BrightMind Toys Inc.

**Email 3**
**From:** Marcus Thorne <m.thorne@example.com>
**To:** support@brightmindtoys.com
**Subject:** RE: RE: Incident with EduPlush-300 - Request for Investigation
**Date:** October 17, 2023

To BrightMind Toys,

I disagree with your assessment. The cover detached due to a manufacturing defect in the screw threads. The threads were stripped. The babysitter did not apply excessive force; the child was handling the toy with both hands.

The marketing was misleading. The "under 3" warning is contradictory to the marketing that targeted 2-5 year olds. This is a safety hazard.

I am requesting that you provide the raw data from the Q2 2023 small parts testing. I also request that you address the supervision issue. The babysitter was adjusting the lighting.

Regards,
Marcus Thorne
